---
title: "How far should it fly?"
---

{{< include _model.qmd >}}

The speed and angle of attack at which the ballasted glider flies itself, then
the still-air glide that follows from them. Trim is solved by iteration because
the two conditions are coupled: the angle where the pitching moment about the CG
vanishes sets the lift coefficient, that sets the speed, and the speed moves the
polar through Reynolds number.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Specified
**Still-air steady glide, released at trim speed** · asked of the user,
2026-08-28 · the aircraft's own performance rather than a measure of anyone's
throwing arm. A thrown launch zooms and may stall, which needs pitch freedom and
is a separate question.

**Release height: 1.5 m** · asked of the user, 2026-08-28 · a normal standing
throw. Range scales linearly with it.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Assumed
Still air, and a glide already settled at trim — no launch transient, no thermal,
no wind. Ballast is at the nose, as the previous entry concluded.
:::

```{python}
H = 1.5                              # m, release height, specified above

x_np = neutral_point()
mp = mass_properties(m_ballast=ballast_for(x_np - 0.10 * c_w, 0.0), x_ballast=0.0)
W = mp.mass * 9.81


t = trim(mp.mass, mp.x_cg)
LD, sink = t["LD"], t["sink"]

# The polars entry's headline figure, recomputed rather than quoted, so this
# entry cannot end up disagreeing with the one it is comparing itself against.
p6 = polars(np.linspace(-15, 15, 121), V=6.0)
LD_6 = float((np.array(p6["CL"]) / np.array(p6["CD"])).max())
```

**Answer.** About `{python} f"{LD*H:.1f}"` m, from a
`{python} f"{H:.1f}"` m release — a glide of
`{python} f"{LD:.2f}"`:1 lasting `{python} f"{H/sink:.1f}"` seconds, sinking at
`{python} f"{sink:.2f}"` m/s. Ballasted to the specified 10% MAC it weighs
`{python} f"{mp.mass*1e3:.2f}"` g and settles at
`{python} f"{t['V']:.2f}"` m/s, nose-up `{python} f"{t['alpha']:.1f}"`°.

That glide ratio is worth reading against the polar the chapter has already
plotted. The best L/D anywhere on it at 6 m/s is
`{python} f"{LD_6:.2f}"` — but the aircraft does not fly there. It trims at
`{python} f"{t['V']:.2f}"` m/s — Reynolds number
`{python} f"{t['Re']:.0f}"` against the `{python} f"{polars(np.array([4.0]), V=6.0)['Re_c']:.0f}"`
the polars are read at — and at a lift coefficient of
`{python} f"{t['CL']:.2f}"`, well above the one that minimises drag. Both effects
push the same way, and the achievable glide is
`{python} f"{(1 - LD/LD_6)*100:.0f}"`% worse than the headline figure. Quoting
the best-L/D number for this aircraft would be quoting a condition it never
reaches.

The trim is a genuine stable equilibrium, not an artefact of the search:
`{python} f"{t['slope']:+.4f}"` per degree through the crossing, so a nose-up
disturbance is pushed back down.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-glide
#| tbl-cap: "The trimmed glide. Everything below the rule follows from the two rows above it and the specified release height."
import pandas as pd

pd.DataFrame({
    "quantity": ["all-up mass", "trim angle of attack", "trim speed",
                 "Reynolds number at trim", "lift coefficient", "drag coefficient",
                 "glide ratio", "sink rate", "range from 1.5 m", "time aloft"],
    "value": [f"{mp.mass*1e3:.2f} g", f"{t['alpha']:.1f}°", f"{t['V']:.2f} m/s",
              f"{t['Re']:.0f}", f"{t['CL']:.3f}", f"{t['CD']:.4f}",
              f"{LD:.2f} : 1", f"{sink:.2f} m/s", f"{LD*H:.1f} m",
              f"{H/sink:.1f} s"],
}).style.hide(axis="index")
```
